🍳 Hello, Saturday! Smart Brevity™ count: 1,355 words ... 5 mins. Erica Pandey is your weekend host. Edited by Katie Lewis.
 
 
1 big thing: Month that changed the market
 
Data: Financial Modeling Prep. Chart: Erin Davis/Axios

As stocks limp to the end of a terrible, horrible, no good, very bad month, the AI trade is in uncharted and highly uncertain new territory.

  • Why it matters: AI exuberance has been driving markets and the economy for the past several years — so it's difficult to overstate the change in the investment environment over just the last few weeks, Axios' Emily Peck and Matt Phillips write.

😨 By the numbers: The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down 11.1% since Nov. 1. Both the Nasdaq and the S&P 500, the benchmark stock index, are now in correction territory — meaning down more than 10% from their most recent highs.

  • The closely watched SOX semiconductor index, which tracks many of the high-flying chip stocks that supercharged markets, is down 21.2% over that same period.
  • Nvidia, the premier stock of the AI trade, is down a shocking 38.4% this month. The stock closed at $125.53 yesterday. In May, it was trading at more than $220.
Lead stories of today's New York Times and Wall Street Journal.

Catch up quick: AI fever was already starting to break heading into November, and then three major headwinds appear to have crushed the vibes.

  1. 🗳️ Americans voted overwhelmingly for AI-skeptical candidates and ballot measures constraining data center construction.
  2. 👀 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who helped fuel the AI infrastructure boom by extending a range of unorthodox financial lifelines to smaller, heavily indebted AI players, resigned amid scandal.
  3. 🤖 AI lab Anthropic listed its shares in the biggest offering of all time. The widely watched milestone failed to lift investor sentiment on tech, and shares continued to tumble.

2. 🏛️ Congress gets a huge makeover
 
Data: House historian, U.S. Senate. Chart: Erin Davis/Axios

Americans want change, and they're about to get it: A perfect storm of congressional retirements, primary upsets, gerrymandering, flipped seats and lawmakers who died in office has created the biggest freshman class in decades, Axios' Justin Green and Kathleen Hunter write.

  • Why it matters: Congress had a 14% approval rating (not a typo) when Gallup polled registered voters in October. That's its lowest pre-midterm number since 1974.

The big picture: The Senate is on track for its biggest freshman class since 1946. In the House, it's shaping up to be the biggest since 1992.

  • Congress is saying goodbye to former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).
  • They've been in Congress since 1981, 1983, 1985 and 1987, respectively.

3. 💡 Optimistic gift for young people
 

Cover: Authors Equity
 

Jim VandeHei calls this the most important book he'll ever write: It's aimed at giving college kids, young workers and all of us a different, more optimistic, actionable way to see and navigate our world.

  • It started as a letter to the Axios CEO's kids, then became a full-fledged plan to maximize your mind, mood and career.
  • "In a world that often makes you feel small and powerless," Jim writes, "the one thing you truly own is you. YOU own what you do, read, share, think, eat and spend your time on. This book shows you how to maximize that mentality. ... You've got this!"

🧀 What's next: Jim will launch an ask-me-anything college tour in January to talk about AI, politics, work, life and the best damn country in the world.

  • Stops include: Indiana, William Penn, Arkansas, Boston College, Stanford, UVA, South Carolina, University of Wisconsin-Oshkosh (Jim's alma mater, UWO!), Maine, Elon and Princeton.

Please email our amazing tour maestro, Madeleine Woolgar, if you want your alma mater — or company — to be part of the mix.

4. 🏎️ Stat du jour: GTA shatters records
 
Image: Rockstar Games

Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79 billion in preorder and Day 1 sales, marking not just the most lucrative video game debut ever, but likely the biggest launch of any creative work in the history of entertainment, Axios' Sara Fischer reports.

  • GTA VI netted more in its debut than the highest-grossing movie ever, "Avengers: Endgame," has earned in its lifetime ($2.9 billion).

5. ⛽ Driving through the pain
 

High gas prices swayed voters, but haven't kept Americans off the roads.

  • Why it matters: Most driving isn't especially optional. So people are just absorbing the cost, Axios' Ben Geman reports.

By the numbers: The Energy Policy Research Foundation finds that American households spent $300 to $730 more on gas from March through August than during the same period last year.

  • But there's "no discernible evidence of a decline in gasoline consumption," UC Berkeley energy economist Lucas Davis writes. "Drivers may talk about cutting back, but studies in the economics literature consistently find that gasoline demand is inelastic in the short run."

6. 🦾 Anthropic savant says he solved math's most famous problem
 

Image via Levent Alpöge
 

A 34-year-old mathematician at Anthropic says he used Claude to solve the 167-year-old Holy Grail of math problems, the Riemann Hypothesis.

  • Why it matters: "For months now, mathematicians have been repeatedly stunned to see machines conquer mathematical problems that have eluded human geniuses for years — in the case of the Riemann Hypothesis, for more than a century and a half," the N.Y. Times reports (gift link).

Levent Alpöge — a Turkish-American and native of Long Island who's a member of Anthropic's technical staff — made the claim with a four-page explanation posted on his website yesterday:

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. ... Claude began to leave me in awe."

Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow toward infinity, AP reports.

  • A day after Anthropic's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the elusive problem.

Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programming language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems.

  • Formally assessing whether the problem has actually been solved will take time. Just 10 weeks ago, OpenAI said its technology took 88 hours to crack the Navier-Stokes equations, which date to the 19th century.

The bottom line: Scientific American says the AI-generated solution to the Riemann Hypothesis, "long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology's year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion."

  • See the four-page paper.
 
 
7. ☎️ Talkin' turkey
 
A screen with thawing and roasting times hangs at the front of the talk line call center. Photo: Carrie Shepherd/Axios

Since 1981, the Butterball Turkey Talk-Line in Naperville, Ill., has answered millions of harried, frustrated and emotional calls (and now texts and chats) with urgent questions about cooking the turkey.

  • The talk line opens at the beginning of November and runs through Christmas Eve every year.

🍗 The talk line started with six home economists on phones with Rolodexes of answers. Now it's about 60 people with earpieces and laptops.

  • Everyone who works there has some food-related degree or training, including chefs, dietitians, food scientists and food stylists, reports Axios Chicago's Carrie Shepherd, who visited the call center this week.

🧊 The No. 1 query? "Some kind of thawing question," talk line supervisor Jessica Romanowski says.

  • Others: "How do I thaw my turkey? ... How long will it take to thaw my turkey? ... Why isn't my turkey thawed yet? ... Oh no, I forgot to start thawing my turkey. How do I do it?"

Thawing and carving tips.
 
 
8. 🍼 1 for the road: Bots name babies
 

Illustration: Maura Losch/Axios
 

AI may have ruined the name Claude. But now parents are turning to it for help naming their babies.

  • Case in point: Baby-naming website Nameberry is already feeling the effects of AI. The site's users and pageviews both fell roughly 40% between October 2025 and October 2026, according to Nameberry co-creator and CEO Pam Redmond.
  • Chatbots are good at suggesting names, Redmond says. But she suspects they could steer more parents toward the same trendy, "middlebrow cool" choices like Sloane and Sutton.

🔮 What's next: Names gaining popularity, per Nameberry's internal search data, include Beatrice, Sabine, Fiona, Ivy, Mae, Marin, Gwendolyn, Murray and Conrad.

  • Others Redmond predicts will take off: Rosemary, Mabel, Archie and Bodie.

By sharing these names, we may have just given the bots a few more to suggest.
